title: Gravitational Potential Energy Far from Earth
short: U = −Gm₁m₂/r, which is zero when the objects are infinitely far apart.
trouble: Students are puzzled that the energy is negative, or use mgh for heights comparable to Earth's radius.

blocks.html: $mgh$ assumes the field $g$ stays the same. For rockets and satellites it doesn't: $g$ weakens with distance from Earth's center. Adding up the work against the full law of gravitation gives a formula that works at any distance, and it comes with a minus sign.
For two masses a distance $r$ apart (center to center), $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$, choosing $U = 0$ when they are infinitely far apart. $U$ rises toward zero as they separate.

Pulling the masses apart takes positive work, because gravity pulls them together, and that work raises $U$. Going outward, the force weakens as $1/r^2$, and the area under the force-distance graph from $r$ out to infinity is finite: $\dfrac{GMm}{r}$. Since $U$ must rise by that much to reach $0$ at infinity, it starts at $-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$. Near the surface, the change between $R$ and $R + h$ is very close to $mgh$.

blocks.name: ph-energy
blocks.cap: U(r) for a 1,000 kg payload, with r in Earth radii: −62.6 GJ at the surface, rising toward 0 far away. With a total energy of −20 GJ (the dashed line) it rises to about 3.1 Earth radii and falls back; only with E ≥ 0 could it escape.

blocks.title: Raising a payload high
blocks.q: How much does $U$ increase when that $1{,}000\ \text{kg}$ payload rises from the surface to $6{,}371\ \text{km}$ up (one Earth radius)?
steps: $mgh$ would give $6.24 \times 10^{10}\ \text{J}$, about twice too much, because $g$ is only a quarter as strong at that height.

blocks.title: Leaving Earth
blocks.q: How much energy must be added to a $1\ \text{kg}$ object at rest on the surface to take it infinitely far away?
steps: $U$ goes from $-\dfrac{GM}{R}$ to $0$, so the energy needed is $$\dfrac{GM}{R} = \dfrac{(6.674 \times 10^{-11})(5.972 \times 10^{24})}{6.371 \times 10^{6}}.$$
That is about $6.26 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J}$, or $62.6\ \text{MJ}$ per kilogram.

blocks.html: Being puzzled by the negative sign, or using $mgh$ when $h$ is comparable to Earth's radius. The sign only reflects the choice of zero at infinity: every finite separation has less energy than that. And $mgh$ assumes constant $g$, which fails far from the surface. Check: $U$ should always increase (become less negative) as $r$ grows.
Try it in the Science Lab's Rocket Builder, where the climb out of Earth's gravity sets how much fuel a rocket needs.
